paragraphs.text: Louisville Cardinals (6-1) vs. Creighton Bluejays (7-1)
Players Era Festival 16 Championship
Game Time: 10:30 p.m.
Location: Michelob ULTRA Arena: Las Vegas, Nev.
Television: ESPN
Announcers: Dan Shulman (play-by-play) and Jay Bilas (analyst)
Favorite: Louisville by 6.5
Series: Creighton leads, 3-1
Last Meeting: Creighton won 89-75 on March 20, 2025 in the NCAA Tournament first round in Lexington, Ky.

About Creighton:

A team that many people thought would go 0-3 in Las Vegas, Creighton instead comes into Saturday night’s Players Era championship game riding a five-game winning streak and looking to continue its early-season resurgence under first-year head coach Alan Huss.

The Bluejays are 7-1 after an impressive run in Vegas that has included wins over Michigan, TCU and No. 22 Gonzaga. Those triumphs, coupled with a neutral court win over Iowa, have helped erase the sting of an 89-82 road loss to a not great Kansas State team.

Named the replacement to longtime head coach Greg McDermott last March, Huss — a Creighton player from 1997-2001 — spent six seasons as an assistant with McDermott from 2017-23 before returning as associate head coach in 2025. He also spent two seasons as the head coach at High Point, compiling a 56-15 record and leading the Panthers to the NCAA Tournament in 2025. His teams at High Point were known for their offensive production, and he inherits a Creighton program that has traditionally been one of the better offensive teams in the country. One of the biggest areas of emphasis under Huss has been creating a more disruptive defensive identity, using length, pressure and activity to force turnovers and make life difficult for opposing offenses.

The biggest offensive weapon for the Bluejays is a player Louisville fans should be familiar with in senior guard Wes Enis. The 6-1 transfer from South Florida is averaging 19.4 points per game and leads the team with 33 made three-pointers.

Enis is the son of former NFL running back and Penn State All-American Curtis Enis, and he has an interesting background beyond that. A self-described “zero-star prospect” coming out of high school in Ohio, Enis took college-credit courses and graduated early from Miami East High School, sacrificing the chance to play his senior season of high school ball. Instead, he enrolled early at Division-II Lincoln Memorial in December of 2023. His intention all along was to prove himself and earn a shot at the D-I level.

Enis scored 1,002 points in just two seasons at Lincoln Memorial, averaging over 20 points per game in his sophomore season. That same year he earned conference Player of the Year and Defensive Player of the Year honors, while also drawing interest from a litany of respected D-I programs. He chose USF, and immediately became the team’s standout scorer in his first and only season with the Bulls.

When he’s on, Enis is just about as dangerous an outside shooter as there is in the country. He isn’t exceptionally quick with the ball in his hands, but he’s quick enough. His handles and his effective twitchiness allowed him to get to the rim consistently against most American Conference defenders, and he’s a crafty finisher once he get there. Enis is also the best mid-range player on the team, and he’s really good at doing that slight arm extension thing (read: uncalled offensive foul) to create space before taking a 10-15 footer.

Enis has been particularly productive during Creighton’s run through the Players Era tournament, scoring 24 against Michigan, 20 against TCU and 28 against Gonzaga. He’s coming into Saturday’s game playing some of the best basketball of his career. He also likely has a chip on his shoulder after declaring before last season’s first round game against Louisville that South Florida was “the better team,” and then proceeding to 2-for-15 from the field and 0-for-11 from three against the Cards.

The other major backcourt weapon for Creighton is BJ Davis, a 6-foot-1 senior transfer from San Diego State. Davis is averaging 16.9 points per game and has been one of the most versatile players on the roster. He’s capable of scoring from the perimeter, attacking the basket and creating opportunities for his teammates. He put together an extraordinary performance in Friday night’s win over Gonzaga, recording 27 points, 11 rebounds and 11 assists for a triple-double. Davis also scored 10 points in overtime, helping the Bluejays pull away after trailing by eight points late in regulation. He’s quickly become one of the most important players on Huss’s roster.

Austin Swartz (8.9 ppg) provides another experienced option in the backcourt. The 6-foot-4 junior can knock down outside shots, handle the basketball and contribute as a secondary playmaker. Freshman Katrelle Harmon (5.6 ppg) has also been an important contributor, particularly as a facilitator. His ability to distribute the basketball gives Huss another option when Davis isn’t initiating the offense. Hudson Greer has provided additional scoring off the bench and is another player capable of hurting opponents from beyond the arc.

Up front, Creighton has an interesting combination of size, athleticism and versatility. Jackson McAndrew, a 6-foot-10 forward, is an especially intriguing player because of his ability to stretch the floor. McAndrew, who I believe is the only primary contributor for Creighton who played in the tournament game against Louisville two years ago, is comfortable operating away from the basket and can create matchup problems for opposing big men. Oswin Erhunmwunse provides a more traditional interior presence, bringing size, rebounding and athleticism around the rim. The Bluejays also have Fredrick King, a 6-foot-10 senior who contributed nine points and nine rebounds in Friday’s win over Gonzaga. Freshman Trevon Carter-Givens gives Huss another big body to work with, while Jasen Green provides additional frontcourt experience and versatility.

One of the most interesting things about this Creighton team is how quickly it has developed an offensive identity under Huss. The Bluejays are averaging 86.3 points per game through eight contests and shooting 37.8% from three-point range. They’ve scored at least 95 points in each of their last three games, including the overtime win against Gonzaga Friday night. They also do a good job sharing the basketball, averaging nearly 18 assists per game. Enis and Davis are the primary scoring options, but Swartz, McAndrew and Greer give them additional players capable of making opponents pay for focusing too much attention on the two leading guards.

Defensively, Huss is trying to establish a more aggressive identity than Creighton has traditionally been known for. The Bluejays are averaging more than 11 steals per game and have forced opponents into considerably more turnovers than they’ve committed themselves. They’re holding opponents to 42.8% shooting from the field and 32.3% from three-point range. The combination of Davis’s perimeter defense, the length of the frontcourt and Huss’s emphasis on creating pressure has helped produce some encouraging early results.

This is a team that can really score out of an offense that is still very similar to the one that torched Louisville two seasons ago. Enis is the player who can get hot in a hurry, while Davis is capable of hurting opponents in several different ways. The Cardinals need to make both players work for their points, avoid allowing easy transition opportunities and keep Creighton’s supporting cast from getting comfortable. Davis’s playmaking ability also makes it important to avoid overcommitting defensively and giving him easy opportunities to find open teammates.

Louisville should also have opportunities to attack Creighton inside and use its athleticism around the basket. The Bluejays have some size, but their offense is driven primarily by their guards, and making them defend physically for 40 minutes should be an important part of the game plan.
Notable:
—A win Saturday night would give Louisville its 32nd regular season tournament championship.
—Louisville and Creighton both earned $500,000 by winning their side of the Players Era bracket. The winner of Saturday night’s game will earn an additional $500,000.

—Louisville has defeated top 15 ranked opponents in three consecutive games for the first time in program history. They are only the fifth team in Division I history to beat three AP top 15 teams in the span of four days.
—All three of Creighton’s wins over Louisville have come in NCAA Tournament games.
—Creighton is 64-180 all-time in games against top 25 teams.
—Louisville is 8-12 against top 25 opponents under Pat Kelsey, but 3-0 so far this season.
—Because of the extra game in Las Vegas, Creighton announced Saturday that it has canceled its Dec. 1 home game against Oral Roberts. Louisville will host Texas in the ACC-SEC Challenge on Dec. 1.
—Louisville is 6-1 in regular season tournament games under head coach Pat Kelsey.

—Creighton is seeking its eighth title in an MTE over the last 25 seasons, but its first since winning the Cayman Islands Classic in 2018. Three of the Bluejays’ five most recent titles came in Las Vegas.
—Creighton is 4-0 in neutral court games so far this season, while Louisville is 3-0. Both teams’ only loss came in a true road game (at Memphis for Louisville, at Kansas State for Creighton).
—Louisville is one of 29 programs in Division I with five or more countries represented on their roster.
—Creighton’s seven wins so far in the month of November have already tied a program record.
—Louisville has a 275-86 record against non-conference opponents over the last 26 seasons.
—Entering Saturday, Creighton has made a three-pointer in 1,098 games in a row, the nation’s 10th-longest active streak.
—Creighton’s 113-game streak of five or more made three-pointers is the nation’s longest active streak.
—Creighton is 1-2 all-time against teams ranked No. 25 in the AP poll.

—The last time Creighton defeated ranked teams in back-to-back games (as well as back-to-back days) was Nov. 21 & Nov. 22, 2022 at the Maui Invitational. Dan Shulman and Jay Bilas, who will call Saturday’s action, broadcast both of those games.
—Louisville is 46-6 under head coach Pat Kelsey when leading at halftime, with one of those losses coming earlier this season against Memphis.
—Louisville is 0-10 under head coach Pat Kelsey when trailing by 5 points or more at halftime.
—Louisville is 56-0 under head coach Pat Kelsey when leading with five minutes to play. The Cardinals are also 1-20 under Kelsey when trailing with five minutes to play.
—Louisville is 14-0 over the past 11 seasons when limiting opponents to no more than one three-point field goal.
—Louisville is 122-0 all-time when scoring 100 or more points in non-overtime games.
—Louisville has won 167 consecutive games when holding an opponent under 50 points.
Ken Pomeroy Prediction: Louisville 82, Creighton 80
